mcqs.q: A literature review is best defined as:
opts: A structured process of finding, evaluating and synthesizing existing evidence
A list of all the articles read during a project
A collection of quotations from the most cited authors
A summary of the results of one landmark study
mcqs.explain: It is explicitly more than a list of articles or a collection of quotations.

mcqs.q: Which question does a STRONG literature review NOT need to answer?
opts: Which journal should the study be submitted to?
What is known and what is uncertain?
What conflicts and what is missing?
Why does the proposed study matter?
mcqs.explain: The five questions concern the state of the evidence and the justification for the new study.

mcqs.q: The first step in conducting a literature review is:
opts: Deciding which citation style to use
mcqs.explain: Without a focused question there is no way to decide what is relevant.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the stated benefits of doing a literature review?
opts: It guarantees that the new study will produce significant results
It helps you avoid repeating previous research
It helps you select the right study design, tools, outcomes and statistical methods
It lets you compare your new findings with previous research
mcqs.explain: It also makes the research question clear and explains why the study is needed.

mcqs.q: A flexible, broad summary of what is known about a topic, written in the author's own words with no strict rules about searching, is a:
mcqs.explain: It is used for the background chapter of a thesis or for preparing a presentation.

mcqs.q: Which review type follows a pre-written protocol, searches many databases thoroughly and critically appraises study quality?
mcqs.explain: It uses predefined search and eligibility criteria and often frames the question with PICO.

mcqs.q: A review that maps what studies exist, what concepts are used and where the gaps are, without judging study quality in detail, is a:
mcqs.explain: It suits a topic that is new or not well defined.

mcqs.q: A streamlined version of a systematic review designed for urgent decisions is a:
mcqs.explain: It is used when evidence is needed quickly for a policy, guideline or clinical decision, or when time or resources are limited.

mcqs.q: “In undergraduate medical students, does simulation-based training improve suturing skills compared to traditional lecture?” is best answered by a:
mcqs.explain: It is a focused comparison question with a clear PICO structure.

mcqs.q: “What is known about simulation in medical education?” is best answered by a:
mcqs.explain: A broad what-exists question calls for a scoping review; a specific does-X-work question calls for a systematic review.

mcqs.q: When choosing the type of review, the two questions to ask are:
opts: What is my question (broad vs specific), and how much time and resources do I have?
Which journal will publish it, and who will be a co-author?
How many databases exist, and which are free?
Which citation style is required, and how many references are needed?
mcqs.explain: The scope of the question and the available resources together determine the appropriate type.

mcqs.q: Which two search resources are described as fully FREE?
mcqs.explain: The Cochrane Library is partially free; Embase, Scopus and Web of Science are subscription-based via an institutional library.

mcqs.q: The Cochrane Library (CENTRAL) is described as:
opts: Partially free, with full access often via institutional subscription
Completely subscription-based with no free content
mcqs.explain: Embase, Scopus and Web of Science are fully subscription-based.

mcqs.q: The relationship between PubMed and MEDLINE is that:
opts: PubMed is a free search interface and MEDLINE is its largest component
MEDLINE is the interface and PubMed is the database inside it
They are two names for exactly the same database
mcqs.explain: MEDLINE uses the controlled vocabulary called MeSH.

mcqs.q: MeSH stands for:
mcqs.explain: It is the controlled vocabulary used by MEDLINE.

mcqs.q: MeSH terms are best compared to:
opts: Hashtags on social media, which group articles about the same topic together
The keywords chosen by the author
The impact factor of the journal
mcqs.explain: They are standardized tags applied by experts, not the author's own words.

mcqs.q: The main advantage of searching with MeSH terms is that:
opts: You can find all articles on a topic even when authors use different words
It restricts results to systematic reviews only
It removes the need to use Boolean operators
mcqs.explain: Heart attack, myocardial infarction and cardiac infarction all carry the single official tag Myocardial Infarction.

mcqs.q: In the worked MeSH example, the single official term applied to articles on heart attack is:
mcqs.explain: Without MeSH you might miss articles that use one of the other wordings.

mcqs.q: The Boolean operator AND:
opts: Narrows the search — both terms must appear
Broadens the search — either term may appear
Groups terms to control the order of operations
mcqs.explain: For example, simulation AND students requires both to be present.

mcqs.q: The Boolean operator OR:
opts: Broadens the search — either term may appear
Narrows the search — both terms must appear
Has no effect on the number of results
mcqs.explain: For example, adolescent OR teenager OR youth widens the pool of synonyms.

mcqs.q: The Boolean operator NOT:
opts: Excludes terms and should be used cautiously
mcqs.explain: It removes the whole record, so an article that merely mentions the excluded term is lost.

mcqs.q: Which search string would BROADEN a search?
mcqs.explain: AND narrows and NOT excludes; only OR broadens.

mcqs.q: Parentheses in a search strategy are used to:
opts: Group terms to control the order of operations, just as in mathematics
Mark a phrase that must be matched exactly
Restrict the search to a date range
mcqs.explain: For example, (cats OR dogs) AND adoption finds either animal first, then combines that pool with adoption.

mcqs.q: In the strategy (cats OR dogs) AND adoption, the system:
opts: Looks for either animal first, then combines that pool with adoption
Looks for adoption first, then filters for cats
Requires cats, dogs and adoption all to appear
mcqs.explain: This is the standard pattern: synonyms joined by OR inside parentheses, concepts joined by AND between them.

mcqs.q: What is the likely effect of the search strategy hypertension NOT pregnancy?
opts: It retrieves articles about both hypertension and pregnancy
It retrieves articles about pregnancy only
mcqs.explain: It also excludes a hypertension paper that merely mentions pregnancy in passing.

mcqs.q: Which search strategy is most appropriate for “What is the effect of physical activity on obesity among adolescents?”
opts: Physical activity AND obesity AND adolescents
Physical activity OR obesity OR adolescents
mcqs.explain: The three main concepts should be combined with AND to retrieve studies addressing all concepts.

mcqs.q: The standard way to build a search strategy from a question is to:
opts: Join synonyms with OR inside parentheses, then join the concepts with AND
Join all terms with AND with no parentheses
Use NOT to remove every unrelated topic
mcqs.explain: For example (adolescent OR teenager OR youth) AND (physical activity) AND (obesity).

mcqs.q: Which review type uses PICO to frame its question?
mcqs.explain: It answers a specific question and follows predefined search and eligibility criteria.

mcqs.q: A student has two weeks to give a seminar on a broad topic for a thesis background chapter. The appropriate review type is:
mcqs.explain: Narrative reviews are explicitly recommended for a thesis background chapter or a presentation.

mcqs.q: A guideline committee needs evidence within days for an urgent clinical decision. The appropriate review type is:
mcqs.explain: The rapid review is a streamlined systematic review designed for urgent decisions when time or resources are limited.

mcqs.q: A reference-management program is software that:
opts: Stores bibliographic details and outputs multiple citation styles
Searches databases and ranks papers by their relevance
Detects plagiarism in a submitted manuscript
Screens studies for inclusion in a systematic review
mcqs.explain: It stores author, title, journal and year, organizes references, and supports APA, Vancouver, Harvard and others.

mcqs.q: Which three are named as common reference-management tools?
mcqs.explain: The second and third groups are AI tools; the fourth are databases.

mcqs.q: In Vancouver style, in-text citations are:
opts: Numbers in brackets or superscript, in order of first mention
Author surname and year in parentheses
The journal title followed by the year
mcqs.explain: The reference list is then numbered in that same order.

mcqs.q: In Harvard and APA styles, the reference list is ordered:
opts: Numerically by order of first citation
By the journal in which each appeared
mcqs.explain: Both are author-date styles, so the list is alphabetical.

mcqs.q: Vancouver style is most widely used in:
mcqs.explain: APA and Harvard are used in many social sciences and some health-related fields.

mcqs.q: Reusing your own previously published work without citing it is:
opts: Acceptable, since the work is your own
mcqs.explain: It is explicitly listed as a form of plagiarism.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as a form of plagiarism?
opts: Paraphrasing too closely without a citation
Quoting with quotation marks and an immediate citation
Citing an idea you arrived at independently
Using a reference manager to format citations
mcqs.explain: Copying without quotation marks, close paraphrase, unattributed figures and self-reuse all count.

mcqs.q: The recommended way to paraphrase properly is to:
opts: Read, understand, set the source aside, then write in your own words
Change every third word while keeping the sentence structure
Translate the passage and then translate it back
Shorten the passage to under twenty-five words
mcqs.explain: And still cite the original idea even when paraphrased.

mcqs.q: When you are unsure whether something needs a citation, you should:
opts: Omit the citation and note the source in an appendix
Cite only if the wording is taken verbatim
Ask whether the idea is widely known in the field
mcqs.explain: This is the stated rule of thumb.

mcqs.q: Predatory journals are characterised by:
opts: Prioritising publication fees over rigorous peer review
Charging no fee but refusing to index their content
Publishing only negative or null results
mcqs.explain: They may also mislead authors about indexing, impact factors or editorial boards.

mcqs.q: Publishing in a predatory journal can:
opts: Improve visibility at the cost of peer review
Count towards indexing in PubMed regardless
Be corrected later by republishing elsewhere
mcqs.explain: Credibility damage and wasted effort are the stated consequences.

mcqs.q: The core principle for using AI in a literature review is to:
opts: Support your thinking, not replace your reading and analysis
Replace manual searching once the question is defined
Generate the first draft and then verify the citations
Use it only for systematic reviews, never narrative ones
mcqs.explain: AI must be used responsibly and ethically, with human oversight and verification.

mcqs.q: Which AI tools are named for discovery and search?
opts: Elicit, Consensus, ResearchRabbit, Litmaps and Connected Papers
mcqs.explain: They suggest keywords, identify related papers and rank by relevance.

mcqs.q: Which AI tool is named for AI-assisted screening in systematic reviews?
mcqs.explain: Elicit is named for data extraction in the same stage.

mcqs.q: An AI tool inventing a reference that does not exist is called:
mcqs.explain: The remedy is to verify every citation in PubMed or your library database and read the original before citing.

mcqs.q: Which AI limitation is addressed by also searching PubMed, Embase and Cochrane?
opts: Incomplete coverage of older, non-English or grey literature
Hallucinated citations that do not exist
The inability to take responsibility for accuracy
mcqs.explain: Traditional databases are used in addition to AI tools.

mcqs.q: Which task can AI NOT do in a literature review?
opts: Develop thematic frameworks and identify research gaps
Suggest search terms based on your research question
Summarise the methods and findings of a paper
Generate a bibliography in a given citation style
mcqs.explain: There is no true synthesis — you must personally synthesise and develop your own critical analysis.

mcqs.q: Who is accountable for the accuracy and ethical use of information in a literature review?
mcqs.explain: AI cannot take responsibility for accuracy, completeness or ethical use.

saqs.q: Define a literature review and explain its role in medical research.
saqs.a: A structured process of finding, evaluating and synthesizing existing evidence relevant to a research question — more than a list of articles or quotations. A strong review answers what is known, what is uncertain, what conflicts, what is missing, and why the study matters. The first step is formulating a focused research question.

ans.text: A structured process of finding, evaluating and synthesizing existing evidence relevant to a research question — more than a list of articles or a collection of quotations. A strong review answers what is known, what is uncertain, what conflicts, what is missing, and why the proposed study matters.

list: Find what is already known and avoid repeating previous research
Make the research question clear, defining the main concepts and variables
Select the right study design, tools, outcomes and statistical methods
Compare new findings with previous research, explaining similarities or differences
Explain why the study is needed and how it will contribute to knowledge

ans.text: The first step is formulating a focused research question.

saqs.q: Differentiate the narrative, systematic, scoping and rapid reviews, with an example of each.
saqs.a: NARRATIVE — flexible broad summary, no strict search rules; for a thesis background or presentation. SYSTEMATIC — structured, answers a specific PICO question, pre-written protocol, many databases, critical appraisal. SCOPING — maps what research exists on a broad topic, identifying concepts and gaps, usually without judging quality. RAPID — a streamlined systematic review for urgent decisions with limited time or resources.

head: Review
What it is
Example
rows: flexible, broad summary written in the author's own words, with no strict rules on searching or inclusion
background chapter of a thesis — what is known about using simulation to teach clinical skills
careful and structured, answering a specific question (often PICO), with a pre-written protocol, thorough multi-database searching, critical appraisal of quality and predefined eligibility criteria
does simulation-based training improve suturing skills compared with traditional lecture?
maps what research exists on a broad topic — what studies, what concepts, where the gaps — usually without judging quality in detail
a new or poorly defined topic — mobile apps to help students learn pharmacology
a streamlined systematic review for urgent decisions when time or resources are limited
evidence for virtual reality to teach anatomy during the pandemic

saqs.q: List the important literature search engines and state how each is accessed.
saqs.a: PubMed/MEDLINE free at pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov · Embase subscription via library · Cochrane Library (CENTRAL) partially free, full access often by subscription · Scopus subscription · Web of Science Core Collection subscription · Google Scholar free at scholar.google.com.

head: Search engine
Access
rows: partially free — full access often via institutional subscription

saqs.q: Explain the relationship between PubMed, MEDLINE and MeSH, and why MeSH terms are useful.
saqs.a: PubMed is a free search interface for biomedical literature. MEDLINE is its largest component and uses a controlled vocabulary, MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) — standardized tags experts apply to every article, like hashtags. Searching MeSH finds all articles on a topic even when authors use different words: 'myocardial infarction', 'cardiac infarction' and 'heart attack' all carry the same tag.

rows: a free search interface for biomedical and life-sciences literature
the largest component of PubMed, using a controlled vocabulary
Medical Subject Headings — a standardized list of medical tags experts use to label every article, like hashtags grouping articles on the same topic

ans.text: Instead of relying on the author's exact words, PubMed uses these official tags, so you find all articles on a topic even when different words are used. Example — 'myocardial infarction', 'cardiac infarction' and 'heart attack' are all tagged with the one official term, Myocardial Infarction.

saqs.q: Explain the Boolean operators and the use of parentheses, with examples.
saqs.a: AND narrows — both terms must appear (simulation AND students). OR broadens — either may appear (adolescent OR teenager OR youth). NOT excludes, used cautiously (diabetes NOT gestational) — it removes the WHOLE record, so a paper merely mentioning the term is lost. PARENTHESES group terms to control order, as in maths: (cats OR dogs) AND adoption. Standard pattern — synonyms with OR inside parentheses, concepts joined with AND.

head: Operator
Effect
Example
rows: excludes — use cautiously, it removes the whole record, so a paper merely mentioning the term is also lost
groups terms to control the order of operations, just as in mathematics

ans.text: Standard pattern — join synonyms with OR inside parentheses, and join the separate concepts with AND. So the effect of physical activity on obesity among adolescents becomes physical activity AND obesity AND adolescents.

saqs.q: Explain what MeSH terms are and why searching with them improves a literature search, using the worked example.
saqs.a: MeSH = MEDICAL SUBJECT HEADINGS — a standardized list of medical 'tags' experts apply to every PubMed article, like hashtags grouping articles on the same topic. PubMed uses the official tag rather than the author's exact words. WORKED EXAMPLE: for 'heart attack', some authors write 'myocardial infarction', others 'cardiac infarction', others 'heart attack'; searching the MeSH term retrieves all of them in one search, instead of guessing and listing every synonym.

ans.text: MeSH = MEDICAL SUBJECT HEADINGS — a standardized list of medical 'tags' that experts use to label every article in PubMed, much like hashtags grouping articles on the same topic. PubMed uses these official tags instead of the author's exact words.

Worked example — searching for a 'heart attack': some authors write myocardial infarction, others cardiac infarction, others heart attack. Searching the MeSH term retrieves all of them in one search, instead of requiring the searcher to guess and list every synonym.

saqs.q: State the two worked search questions from the lecture and give the answers with the reasoning.
saqs.a: Q1 'hypertension NOT pregnancy' → C, it EXCLUDES RECORDS CONTAINING PREGNANCY. The hidden cost: a hypertension paper that merely mentions pregnancy in passing is also excluded, because NOT removes the whole record. Q2 'What is the effect of physical activity on obesity among adolescents?' → B, PHYSICAL ACTIVITY AND OBESITY AND ADOLESCENTS — the three main concepts combined with AND retrieve studies addressing all of them.

saqs.q: What is a reference-management program, what does it do, and name three examples.
saqs.a: Software that stores bibliographic details such as author, title, journal and year. It organizes references and supports multiple citation styles including APA, Vancouver and Harvard. Common tools are Zotero, Mendeley and EndNote.

list: Stores bibliographic details — author, title, journal, year.
Organizes references.
Supports multiple citation styles — APA, Vancouver, Harvard and others.

saqs.q: Compare the Vancouver, APA and Harvard citation styles.
saqs.a: Vancouver is numeric: in-text numbers in brackets or superscript in order of first mention, with the reference list numbered in the same order, and it is widely used in biomedical and clinical journals. APA and Harvard are author-date: in-text author and year, with the reference list alphabetical by author surname, used in many social sciences and some health-related fields.

head: Style
In-text
Reference list
rows: numbers in brackets or superscript, in order of first mention
similar author-date form, with small variations

ans.text: Vancouver is the style of biomedical and clinical journals; APA and Harvard are used in many social sciences and some health-related fields.

saqs.q: Define plagiarism, list what it includes, and state how to avoid it.
saqs.a: Using someone else's ideas, words, data or work without proper acknowledgment. It includes copying text without quotation marks or citation, paraphrasing too closely without citation, using figures, tables or data without permission and citation, and reusing your own previous work without citation, which is self-plagiarism. Avoid it by taking clear notes with full source details, using quotation marks for exact wording and citing immediately, paraphrasing properly by reading, understanding, setting the source aside and writing in your own words while still citing, using a reference manager, checking with plagiarism-detection tools, and over-citing rather than under-citing when in doubt.

list: Copying text without quotation marks or citation.
Paraphrasing too closely without citation.
Using figures, tables or data without permission and citation.
Reusing your own previous work without citation — self-plagiarism.
Take clear notes and record full source details.
Use quotation marks for exact wording and cite immediately.
Paraphrase properly — read, understand, set the source aside, write in your own words, and still cite.
Use a reference manager to insert citations consistently.
Check with plagiarism-detection tools if available.
When in doubt, over-cite rather than under-cite.

saqs.q: What are predatory journals and why do they matter?
saqs.a: Journals that prioritize publication fees over rigorous peer review and editorial standards. They may mislead authors about indexing, impact factors or editorial boards. Publishing in such journals can damage credibility and waste effort.

saqs.q: Describe the four stages at which AI can assist a literature review, with examples.
saqs.a: Discovery and search: suggesting keywords and search terms, identifying related papers and ranking by relevance, using Elicit, Consensus, ResearchRabbit, Litmaps, Connected Papers and Scite. Summarization: summarising the research question and methods, key findings and conclusions, and strengths and limitations, using SciSpace, Scite and Elicit. Organization and reference management: tagging and categorizing papers by theme and generating bibliographies in different styles, using Zotero with AI plugins, Mendeley and EndNote. Screening and data extraction for systematic reviews: prioritizing papers for screening, suggesting inclusion and exclusion decisions with human verification, and extracting data fields such as study design, sample size and outcomes, using Rayyan and Elicit.

Elicit, Consensus, ResearchRabbit, Litmaps, Connected Papers, Scite

saqs.q: List the limitations of AI in literature reviews and how each is addressed.
saqs.a: Hallucinations, where AI invents references or misattributes findings, addressed by verifying every citation in PubMed or your library database and reading the original paper before citing. Incomplete coverage, missing older, non-English or grey literature, addressed by also using PubMed, Embase and Cochrane. No true synthesis, since AI cannot develop thematic frameworks, identify gaps or create analytical connections, so you must synthesise personally. Outdated knowledge from model cutoffs, addressed by checking publication dates and searching recent papers manually. No accountability, since AI cannot take responsibility, so you are fully accountable for everything in your review.
